transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-24
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Summary: quick technical deep dive to scope an autoscaling approach combining preemptible instances, reserved GPUs, and on-prem VPC peering for Polaris Networks. Focus areas: tail latency, KV cache warmup, batching strategies, quantized inference tradeoffs, and failure modes for burst traffic.

Topics: hybrid pool topology, preemptible eviction behavior, queueing backpressure, warm KV cache priming, quantization vs quality degradation, SLOs and observability hooks.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex (AE): okay everybody thanks for hopping on. we wanted to go a bit deep into the autoscaling approach you mentioned in the RFP, specifically the idea of mixing preemptible capacity with reserved GPUs and some on-prem nodes, and how that affects KV cache, latency and cost.
[00:14] Priya (SRE): yep, thanks Alex. our main constraint is we have a lot of bursty nights — peak is like 10x baseline — and procurement for more reserved hardware is slow. so we want to know if preemptible + reserved can meet a 95ms p95 for 512-token gen and a 600ms p99 for 2k token workflows.
[00:33] Samira (SE): okay that's a helpful SLO. a few quick clarifying q's: are the 512-token requests mostly short chat turns, and 2k mostly batch summarization? and do you have any hard latency windows where we must tail off instead of queueing?
[00:47] Markus (ML Platform): mostly yes — chat 512 tokens, summarization and codegen go longer. we have some strict SLAs for interactive chat in EU region only. for summarization we can tolerate longer; but the p99 target is still important.
[01:03] Jordan (Sol Eng): also are you planning to route traffic cross-region if there is capacity shortage? or keep EU pinned?
[01:12] Emily (PM): prefer EU-pinned for data residency reasons; routing fallback to other regions requires legal signoff so we want on-prem and reserved in EU first.
[01:23] Samira (SE): got it. so hybrid topology will be EU reserved pool + EU preemptible spot pool + on-prem private pool that talks via VPC. the main tradeoffs: preemptible evictions cause KV cache cold starts and spike tail latency; reserved helps steady-state throughput. on-prem gives you data residency and lower network hop but may have lower elastic scale.
[01:48] Diego (Infra): question on the KV cache: how can we avoid cold-cache storms when evictions happen? if preemptible nodes get reclaimed, we could get a cascade of cache misses.
[02:00] Samira (SE): good point. Redwood supports prefix and KV cache sharding + async KV warming. we can do a few levers: 1) gradual draining: mark preemptible instances as draining and gracefully shift active sessions to reserved/on-prem; 2) cross-tier cache replication for hot keys (small set of user prefixes) so when a preemptible is reclaimed, the reserved pool still has top-k keys; 3) request hedging/fanout: for critical requests, duplicate to reserved pool with first response wins — costlier but keeps latency tight.
[02:36] Alex (AE): can you sketch the queueing model you'd recommend for a 10x burst with 60s peak window?
[02:43] Samira (SE): yes. imagine a two-queue system: a fast lane served by reserved/on-prem with strict concurrency caps per GPU, and a burst lane that feeds preemptible pools with elastic concurrency. implement earliest-deadline-first for the fast lane, and a backpressure gate: if fast-lane backlog > threshold, new short-chat requests are admitted to reserved only up to concurrency; beyond that we allow best-effort where we either queue for up to X ms or spill to a degraded model profile (quantized / lower-seq-length).
[03:18] Priya (SRE): what do you mean by degraded model profile? are we talking int8 quantized variants?
[03:24] Samira (SE): yes — two quick options: 1) quantized variant (int8/awq-type) on preemptible nodes for cheaper tokens but slightly noisier answers, or 2) a distilled smaller model for very latency-sensitive paths. Redwood's routing policy can specify quality thresholds so that for certain customers you never route to lower-quality models.
[03:45] Priya (SRE): our compliance team will be picky about model distortion for financial use-cases; quantization is okay only if we have regression evals.
[03:54] Alex (AE): that's reasonable — Redwood Optimize can run automated evals on your prompt set to estimate MRR/semantic drift for int8 vs float16 and provide a recommended fallback. we'll include that in the playback.
[04:08] Markus (ML Platform): the preemptible eviction pattern from our cloud provider is usually 2 minutes notice with a 30s drain window, but sometimes it's abrupt. how much of a hole does that leave in KV cache?
[04:20] Samira (SE): depends on the working set. if your hot-key ratio is high, evictions can cause measurable P99 spikes. one mitigation is to move hot-key cache to reserved nodes only — essentially a small, persistent cache tier (on reserved GPUs or even CPU-based memcached), while using preemptible for compute statelessly. that reduces memory pressure on ephemeral GPUs.
[04:46] Diego (Infra): so you're suggesting a multi-tier cache: persistent hot-key store + ephemeral local KV for session-level caches?
[04:54] Samira (SE): exactly. persistent hot-key store holds embeddings or prefix tokens for the 1% of keys that account for 60% of traffic. ephemeral local KV holds per-request KV for recent seqs to speed autoregressive passes; losing ephemeral KV is painful but recoverable.
[05:11] Jordan (Sol Eng): how does batching play in? if we have many short chat tokens, we want small batch sizes to keep latency low, but that increases GPU inefficiency. can Redwood dynamically adjust batch target sizes per pool?
[05:24] Samira (SE): yes — runtime has adaptive batching: it maintains separate batching windows per pool and target latency constraints. reserved pool can have slightly larger batching windows since it's lower risk; preemptible pool uses aggressive micro-batching to reduce p99. Redwood also supports multi-tenant batch packing to fill GPU mats without increasing individual latencies beyond the SLO.
[05:48] Emily (PM): multi-tenant batch packing, does that raise data isolation concerns?
[05:54] Samira (SE): good callout — it's only allowed if tenant policy permits. for strict isolation, you can reserve dedicated instances for sensitive customers. Redwood's routing policy has tags for isolation vs cost-savings.
[06:06] Priya (SRE): can we get concrete numbers: if we keep 30% reserved capacity and 70% preemptible, what is expected p95 for 512 tokens?
[06:16] Alex (AE): Samira, maybe you can do a back-of-envelope based on our benchmark curves?
[06:20] Samira (SE): rough ballpark: for a 512-token seq on mid-sized A100-equivalent reserved instances, p95 ~40-60ms when not overloaded. If 30% reserved covers steady-state 1x traffic, and you get a 10x burst, the preemptible micro-batches will add 50-200ms extra depending on cache warmup and queueing. so P95 could jump above your 95ms target unless we do hedging or keep higher reserved headroom.
[06:50] Markus (ML Platform): so to meet 95ms consistently we likely need either higher reserved commit or aggressive hedging that sends duplicates to reserved nodes, correct?
[06:58] Samira (SE): yes — either increase reserved to cover peak concurrency for the 95ms SLO, or use duplicative hedging + fast fallback to a quantized variant. Duplicates increase cost but are predictable. Another trick is to pre-warm pools based on traffic forecasts (scheduled warmups) for predictable nightly surges.
[07:17] Diego (Infra): about pre-warm: does Redwood support running warmup jobs that preload KV cache and model weights on preemptible nodes ahead of a predicted surge?
[07:25] Samira (SE): yes — we have scheduled warmup tasks and also a priority prefetch API. you can feed a list of prefixes or sessions to pre-warm; the system will load KV and prime attention caches. this reduces first-token latency significantly but obviously costs some cycles.
[07:41] Priya (SRE): what's the cost tradeoff? warmup vs always-on reserved?
[07:46] Samira (SE): depends on burst characteristics. for short frequent bursts, reserved is cheaper. for infrequent long bursts, preemptible with warmup is cheaper. we can model your 90-day traffic and build a cost curve; Redwood has an Optimize report for that.
[08:00] Alex (AE): let's talk about network hops — EU on-prem pools connecting to Redwood control plane — does that add nontrivial tail latency?
[08:08] Jordan (Sol Eng): also KMS calls for decryption of model keys — where do those happen?
[08:12] Samira (SE): KMS calls can be done via your KMS in VPC — if your HSM/KMS is on-prem, initial key unwrap may add 10-50ms but it's cached. model shard replication and KV cache access across VPC has a few ms RTT if peered in-region. the heavier latency is model op + memcopy on GPU. network usually isn't the dominant factor unless you are cross-region.
[08:38] Olga (Security): we need to confirm that preemptible nodes won't leak ephemeral cache to other tenants. is memory zeroing enforced on eviction?
[08:45] Samira (SE): yes — instance teardown path includes memory scrub and GPU memory zeroing hooks. Redwood supports tenant isolation at kernel level; we also provide audit logs for evictions and scrubs. we'll attach the security checklist.
[08:58] Priya (SRE): are there best practices for autoscaling policies? we have usage spikes that are both sudden and slow-growing.
[09:06] Samira (SE): recommended hybrid policy: telemetry-driven autoscale for gradual changes (CPU/GPU util, queue length) plus an event-driven burst policy triggered by upstream signals (e.g., ingress surge). implement a cool-down and dampening window; for sudden spikes, use pre-warmed cap where reserved keeps a small buffer of idle pre-warmed workers. configure eviction-aware drain so preemptible nodes are placed into 'drain' on notice.
[09:34] Markus (ML Platform): what about graceful degradation? we want to avoid 500s — prefer serving a smaller model or partial response.
[09:41] Samira (SE): Redwood can define fallbacks: return cached answer, switch to distilled model, or return best-effort partial tokens. also have circuit-breaker thresholds: if queue latency crosses X, drop into degraded mode to keep overall availability.
[09:58] Alex (AE): any concerns about quantization affecting regulatory outputs?
[10:02] Olga (Security): yes we need to log when a response was served by quantized model versus full precision. is that visible in audit traces?
[10:08] Samira (SE): yes — every response has metadata indicating model variant, quantization level, pool route, and runtime cost. Redwood Console can alert on model-regression metrics and tie evals to specific rollouts.
[10:22] Emily (PM): if we run hedging, do we pay for both responses always? how does billing work?
[10:27] Alex (AE): hedging counts both compute runs; Redwood can surface per-token cost and you can set cost caps. hedging is usually used for small high-priority fraction rather than everything.
[10:35] Priya (SRE): a practical question: what's the recommended preemptible/reserved ratio for initial pilot? we can increase later.
[10:42] Samira (SE): for pilot I'd suggest 50/50 with a small reserved buffer for critical low-latency traffic — that gives you cost savings while keeping headroom. monitor P95/P99 and then either shift to 60/40 reserved or introduce hedging based on observed deltas.
[10:57] Markus (ML Platform): can Redwood run a synthetic 48-hour test that replays our traffic traces and injects preemptible evictions to measure tail behavior?
[11:04] Samira (SE): yes — Redwood's bench harness can replay annotated traces, simulate evictions at arbitrary rates, and produce per-route latency/cost breakdowns. we'll need your trace in a specific JSON format.
[11:17] Priya (SRE): we'll export traffic + session traces and scrub PII.
[11:21] Alex (AE): perfect. let's talk about rollout plan then. idea: 1) sandbox bench with 50/50 pools + quantized preemptible; 2) run 48hr replay with synthetic evictions; 3) tune pooling thresholds and hedging; 4) run limited pilot for EU chat in production with monitoring.
[11:39] Emily (PM): timeline?
[11:41] Alex (AE): Samira and I can prepare bench configs by Friday. then we need Polaris to provide traces by Monday. bench runs Tue-Wed, then review Thu.
[11:50] Olga (Security): please include SOC2 artifacts and data retention policies in the packet. also confirm KMS flow and audit logs.
[11:58] Alex (AE): will do. Samira anything else?
[12:01] Samira (SE): one last note — watch out for long KV cache keys. if you have very long prefix tokens, they bloat KV and make shard distribution tricky. consider tokenizing prefixes or reducing persistent KV size for long sessions.
[12:15] Priya (SRE): good to know.
[12:18] Alex (AE): great, thanks everyone. I'll recap action items in the email and attach the bench template.
[12:25] Emily (PM): thanks all.
[12:29] Meeting end.
